objective: By the end of this lesson you can spot the common engine, electrical, instrument, flap, gear, trim, fire and door problems, say what causes them, and run the right checklist while still flying the airplane.
why: Most malfunctions in a light airplane are not deadly by themselves. What hurts pilots is losing control while distracted or startled by the problem, so you need a plan before it happens.

warmup: You are in cruise and the ammeter needle swings to the minus side. Nothing else seems wrong. How long do you think the battery will keep the radios and lights running, and what would you turn off first?

key_terms.def: Ice that forms in the carburetor venturi and on the throttle valve from fuel vaporization and low pressure. It chokes off power.
Uncontrolled, explosive burning of the fuel-air mixture in the cylinder. Causes high cylinder head temperature.
The mixture lights before the spark, usually from a hot spot in the cylinder.
Shows if the alternator is charging the battery (plus) or the battery is being drained (minus).
Turning off electrical equipment you don't need so the battery lasts longer.
A backup static port, often inside the cabin, used when the outside static port is blocked.
When one glass display fails, flight data is shown on the remaining display.
One flap moves and the other does not. The airplane rolls toward the wing with less flap.
Wrong position, speed, attitude or configuration, or a confusing, high-workload situation with reduced safety margins.
An automatic reflex (muscle jerk, raised heart rate) to a sudden, intense, unexpected event.

chunks.title: Partial or complete power loss: causes

body.p: In a piston airplane most power problems come from the induction system, fuel, mixture, combustion or ignition. Know the ones in your engine.

**Carburetor ice.** Fuel vaporizing and low pressure in the venturi make a sharp temperature drop. Ice forms near the throttle valve and venturi, restricts the mixture, and reduces power. Enough ice can stop the engine [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]]. It is most likely below 70 °F (21 °C) with relative humidity above 80 percent, but it can happen at up to 100 °F (38 °C) and humidity as low as 50 percent [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

bullets: First sign with a fixed-pitch prop: rpm drops, maybe followed by roughness. With a constant-speed prop: manifold pressure drops, rpm stays the same [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
Fix: full carburetor heat right away, and leave it full until normal power returns. Roughness from melting ice can last 30 seconds to several minutes. Don't reduce the heat early [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
Carb heat costs power, sometimes up to 15 percent [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
Fuel injection has less icing risk, but impact ice can block the air intake [[1:172|PHAK 7-12]].

body.p: **Fuel problems.** Running a tank dry stops the engine, and air in the lines can cause vapor lock that makes a restart hard [[1:186|PHAK 7-26]]. Water is the main fuel contaminant; in warm weather it can flow into the carburetor and stop the engine [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]]. Never use a lower fuel grade than specified; it can cause detonation [[1:187|PHAK 7-27]]. Fuel starvation remains a leading factor in accidents [[24:345|AFH 17-11]].

**Mixture.** Too rich at altitude fouls plugs and causes roughness and power loss. Too lean (for example, not enriching in a descent) can cause detonation, roughness, overheating and power loss [[1:169|PHAK 7-9]].

**Detonation and preignition.** Both cause high engine temperature and less power, and they are hard to tell apart [[1:180|PHAK 7-20]]. Common causes of detonation: low fuel grade, high manifold pressure with low rpm, high power with a too-lean mixture, and long ground runs or steep climbs [[1:179|PHAK 7-19]].
**Ignition.** If one magneto fails, the other keeps the engine running with a slight power loss [[1:175|PHAK 7-15]].
The AFH table below links engine gauge readings to likely causes and fixes. The POH comes first [[24:365|AFH 18-16]].

check.q: Fixed-pitch prop, cruise, humid 60 °F day. RPM slowly drops. What do you suspect and do?
check.a: Carburetor ice. Apply full carb heat and leave it on until power returns; expect it to run rough for a while as ice melts [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

body.p: Most in-flight electrical failures are in the alternator or generator. After that, the battery is the only source, and it may not last long [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

head: Gauge reading
Meaning
rows: Ammeter minus
More current drawn from the battery than replaced [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]
Ammeter full-scale minus
Alternator/generator malfunction [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]
Ammeter full-scale plus
Voltage regulator malfunction [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]
Low-voltage / ALT warning light
Generator or alternator malfunction (some airplanes have no ammeter) [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]]

body.p: How long will the battery last? More load drains it faster. A 25 amp-hour battery could give 5 amps for 5 hours, but at 10 amps it might last only 2 hours, and a 40-amp load might empty it in about 10 or 15 minutes. An old battery or a late-detected failure means less time [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

bullets: Shed all but the most needed equipment right away [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].
Tell ATC immediately; ask for vectors to the nearest suitable airport [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].
Electric flaps and gear use a lot of power. On a weak battery, selecting them may kill all power at once. Plan a no-flap landing and a manual gear extension [[24:362|AFH 18-13]] [[24:363|AFH 18-14]].
Land at the nearest suitable airport; don't continue the flight [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].

callout.text: In a glass-cockpit airplane, the PFD, AHRS and air data computer all need electrical power. An alternator failure there is an emergency, not just an abnormality [[23:331|IFH 11-6]]. Some have a standby battery that must be ARMED before departure [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

Night VFR requires spare fuses (one spare set, or three of each kind) accessible to the pilot in flight [[35:397|14 CFR 91.205(c)(6)]]. Circuit breakers do the same job as fuses but can be reset [[1:191|PHAK 7-31]].

check.q: Your ALT light comes on and the ammeter shows discharge. Name your first three actions.
check.a: Shed nonessential electrical load, tell ATC and ask for vectors to the nearest suitable airport, and plan for no flaps and a manual gear extension if they are electric [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. Follow the POH alternator checklist.

chunks.title: Vacuum system and gyro instrument failure

body.p: In many trainers an engine-driven vacuum pump spins the attitude and heading indicators. The turn coordinator is often electric, so you still have a source of bank information if one power source fails [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]]. Normal suction is usually between 4.5 "Hg and 5.5 "Hg [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]].

When suction drops below normal, the gyro instruments may become unstable and inaccurate. Some airplanes have a low-vacuum warning light; many small airplanes have none, so scan the suction gauge [[1:218|PHAK 8-16]] [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

In the picture the airplane is really level at 2,000 feet. The attitude indicator shows a left bank, but the turn coordinator, altimeter and VSI disagree. A pilot who misses the failure flags may roll into a real bank chasing a false one [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

bullets: Spot it: compare the attitude indicator with the turn coordinator and VSI [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].
Keep control first, then find the failed part [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].
Cover the failed instruments so they don't fool you [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].
Tell ATC; declare an emergency if needed [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

check.q: Your attitude indicator shows a 20° left bank, but the turn coordinator wings are level and the heading isn't changing. What is happening?
check.a: Probably a vacuum failure. Cross-check the turn coordinator and VSI, cover the failed instruments, keep wings level using the working ones, and check the suction gauge [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].

body.p: Ice, dirt or insects can block the pitot tube or static ports [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]]. A blocked pitot tube affects only the airspeed indicator. A blocked static port affects the airspeed indicator, altimeter and VSI [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].

bullets: Pitot blocked, drain hole open: airspeed drops to zero [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]].
Pitot and drain hole both blocked: airspeed acts like an altimeter, reading higher as you climb and lower as you descend [[1:212|PHAK 8-10]] [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].
Static blocked: altimeter freezes, VSI reads zero, airspeed reads low above the blockage altitude and high below it [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].
A partial static blockage may not show up until you start down. Then the instruments say too high, too fast, and descending too slowly [[24:363|AFH 18-14]] [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

body.p: **Fix:** in visible moisture use pitot heat if equipped [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. If you suspect a static problem, open the alternate static source while climbing or descending; if the needles jump, use it for the rest of the flight [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. Cabin static pressure is lower than outside, so check the POH for corrections [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

**Glass cockpits.** Many glass panels share the same pitot-static inputs with the backup instruments, so both can fail together. Some combine the air data computer and AHRS, so a blockage can even affect attitude [[24:364|AFH 18-15]]. Failure indications are not standardized; learn your system [[24:364|AFH 18-15]] [[24:365|AFH 18-16]].

If a display fails, the system can go to reversionary mode and show flight data on the other screen [[23:329|IFH 11-4]] [[24:345|AFH 17-11]]. If both are lost, you have the standby attitude indicator, altimeter, airspeed indicator and magnetic compass [[23:331|IFH 11-6]].

callout.text: Keep following your position on a chart even with a moving map. If the screen dies, you still know where you are and where the nearest airport is [[23:329|IFH 11-4]].

check.q: During a descent the altimeter seems stuck and the VSI shows zero. What do you do?
check.a: Suspect a blocked static system [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]]. Open the alternate static source; if the needles move, keep using it and apply the POH corrections [[24:364|AFH 18-15]].

head: Problem
What you see
What to do
rows: No flaps
Higher nose attitude, harder to lose altitude, long float [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Wider, longer pattern; expect up to 50 percent more landing distance [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]; don't force it on fast or over-flare [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Split flap
Strong roll toward the wing with less flap [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Opposite aileron and rudder; higher approach speed; no crosswind from the deployed-flap side; fly it on, don't flare hard [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]
Gear won't extend
A gear leg won't respond to the normal or alternate extension method [[24:361|AFH 18-12]]
Try the POH normal and alternate extension. If it still fails, plan a gear-up landing at an airport with crash and rescue; ask for emergency equipment [[24:361|AFH 18-12]]

bullets: Smooth hard runway usually does less damage than rough grass, but sparks can light fuel [[24:361|AFH 18-12]].
Burn off extra fuel to reduce landing speed and fire risk [[24:361|AFH 18-12]].
One main gear up: land nose-high and wings level, hold the unsupported wing up with aileron, then use full opposite rudder and braking [[24:361|AFH 18-12]].
Nosewheel up: hold the nose off, then let it settle slowly; avoid braking [[24:361|AFH 18-12]].

body.p: **Trim.** Trim tabs can save you: if the elevator linkage fails, trim can still raise or lower the elevator enough for a safe landing [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]. The reverse problem is runaway electric trim. Quickly assess it, press the trim disconnect (if installed) or pull the trim circuit breaker, then hold pitch by hand. Depending on control forces, you may need a no-flap landing [[24:348|AFH 17-14]]. Runaway trim and asymmetric flaps can cause an upset directly [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

callout.text: Split flap = roll toward the SHORT flap. Stop the flap, then fight the roll with aileron and the yaw with rudder.

check.q: You select flaps 20 on downwind and the airplane rolls hard right. What happened and what next?
check.a: Asymmetric (split) flap; the right flap has less deflection [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]. Hold wings level with opposite aileron and rudder, fly a faster approach, avoid a crosswind from the deployed-flap side, and fly it onto the runway [[24:360|AFH 18-11]].

head: Type
Clues and causes
First actions (unless the POH says otherwise)
rows: Engine fire
Fuel, oil or hydraulic fluid on a hot surface; smoke/flames from the cowling, or cowling skin discolored, bubbling or melting [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]
Mixture idle cutoff, fuel selector OFF, ignition left ON to burn off fuel in the lines. Don't restart [[24:358|AFH 18-9]]
Electrical fire
Smell of burning insulation [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Find the bad circuit (breakers, avionics, lights). If you can't, turn battery master and alternator OFF if flight conditions permit [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Cabin fire
Smoking, electrical system, or heating system [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]
Fight the fire and get on the ground fast. Use the extinguisher first, then open vents to clear smoke [[24:359|AFH 18-10]]

bullets: Thick black smoke suggests an oil-fed fire; bright orange flames suggest fuel [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].
Some checklists say master OFF, but that also kills radios and the transponder. Unless the fire is electrical or a crash landing is imminent, consider leaving it on [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].
If smoke gets worse when you open the vents, close them right away [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
On some airplanes, lowering gear or flaps can make cabin smoke worse [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
A fire that seems out can rekindle. The airplane may be badly damaged. It is expendable; the people are not [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

body.p: If you must have electrical power after an electrical fire: master OFF, all switches OFF, master ON, then turn on needed switches one at a time with a pause after each, watching for smoke or smell. This can recreate the fire, so the best plan is to land as soon as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].
An emergency descent may be needed. Bank about 30 to 45° to keep positive G, and don't exceed VNE, VLE or VFE [[24:357|AFH 18-8]].

callout.text: Exhaust contains carbon monoxide, which is odorless and colorless [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]. The exhaust system must be free of cracks [[1:178|PHAK 7-18]]; a defective exhaust heating system risks carbon monoxide poisoning, power loss and fire [[1:189|PHAK 7-29]].

check.q: You smell burning insulation in cruise. What is your first move?
check.a: Suspect an electrical fire. Try to find and isolate the bad circuit; if you can't, and conditions permit, turn the battery master and alternator off, then land as soon as possible [[24:359|AFH 18-10]].

chunks.title: Oxygen, ice protection and open doors

body.p: **Supplemental oxygen.** Check the system before every flight: supply, mask and tubing, regulator, gauges and flow indicators. No smoking, and keep oil and grease away [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]]. A cannula flow detector should be in your scan [[1:198|PHAK 7-38]].

head: Cabin pressure altitude
Oxygen rule [[35:401|14 CFR 91.211]]
rows: Above 12,500 ft up to and including 14,000 ft MSL
Required crew must use it for any part of the flight at those altitudes over 30 minutes
Above 14,000 ft MSL
Required crew must use it the entire flight time at those altitudes
Above 15,000 ft MSL
Each occupant must be provided with it

body.p: **Pressurization.** The main danger of decompression is hypoxia. Use oxygen quickly and make a rapid descent [[1:197|PHAK 7-37]].

**Ice protection.** Most light airplanes have only pitot heat and are not certified for icing; they must exit icing conditions right away [[1:200|PHAK 7-40]]. Deice and anti-ice gear should be checked before you meet ice, and it is not meant for long flight in icing [[1:201|PHAK 7-41]]. If a prop boot fails to heat one blade, severe vibration can result [[1:201|PHAK 7-41]]. Electric windshield heat can cause compass errors up to 40° [[1:201|PHAK 7-41]].
**Door opens in flight.** The door rarely hurts the airplane. Pilot distraction does [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

bullets: Fly the airplane first [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].
After liftoff, don't rush to land: climb to pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern and landing [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].
Keep belts on. Leave the door alone; close it on the ground [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].
Use the landing checklist [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

check.q: The cabin door pops open just after liftoff. What do you do?
check.a: Keep flying the airplane, climb to pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern and land. Don't unbuckle or reach for the door [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

chunks.title: Fly it step by step: handling any malfunction

body.p: The POH procedures come first; the AFH gives generic guidance only [[24:350|AFH 18-1]]. Use this order on the checkride and in real life:

bullets: 1. **Fly the airplane.** Keep attitude, airspeed and altitude under control. In an emergency landing, positive control on final has priority over configuration and checklist tasks [[24:353|AFH 18-4]].
2. **Recognize and confirm.** Cross-check instruments and other cues; one indication can be wrong [[24:110|AFH 5-5]] [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].
3. **Immediate action items from memory**, then find the emergency checklist quickly [[24:348|AFH 17-14]].
4. **Run the checklist** to make sure nothing was missed [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].
5. **Talk.** Tell ATC; declare an emergency if needed. Squawk 7700 if you can't reach ATC right away [[34:46|AIM 6-3-2]].
6. **Land** as the checklist and situation call for (e.g., nearest suitable airport after an alternator failure [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]).

head: ACS standard
What the examiner looks for
rows: ACS PA.IX.C.S1
Determine appropriate action for simulated emergencies specified by the evaluator, from at least three of the elements or sub-elements listed in K1 through K5.
ACS PA.IX.C.S2
Complete the appropriate checklist(s).

callout.text: Practice: sit in the airplane with the POH and touch each control in every emergency checklist. Have your CFI call out failures (ALT light, vacuum, door, smoke) and talk through them aloud.

check.q: Why do some pilots do memory items first and read the checklist after?
check.a: Checklists need not be do-lists; you can do the actions, then use the checklist to confirm all were done [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]. Pilots should know immediate action items from memory and find the procedures fast [[24:348|AFH 17-14]].

chunks.title: Risk: checklists, distraction, undesired states and startle

body.p: **Checklist use.** Checklists are of no value if you don't use them; pilots who rely only on memory make errors [[24:36|AFH 1-15]]. The manufacturer's checklists and emergency procedures are a basic defense against threats, errors and undesired aircraft states [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].

**Distraction.** A malfunction can cause an upset simply by pulling your attention away from flying [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. When task demands exceed your ability, control can be lost; a vacuum failure at night in IMC is one example [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Budget time, prioritize tasks and slow down; you can ask ATC for more time [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]. A passenger can help read a checklist [[30:46|RMH 6-3]].

**Undesired aircraft state.** Wrong position, speed, attitude or configuration, a confusing high-workload situation, or reduced safety margins [[30:46|RMH 6-3]]. Example: chasing a failed attitude indicator into a real bank. When defenses fail, your flying skills are the last resort [[30:47|RMH 6-4]].

**Startle and surprise.** Startle is an automatic reflex to a sudden, intense, unexpected event. Untrained pilots often react this way to upsets [[24:108|AFH 5-3]]. Untrained pilots react with abrupt, purposeless control inputs [[24:109|AFH 5-4]]. Scenario-based training with realistic distractions builds protection [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].

callout.text: Startled? Hands steady, eyes on the attitude, fly first. Then name the problem, then the checklist.

check.q: What is the most common way a minor malfunction turns into an accident?
check.a: The pilot gets distracted and loses control. An open door accident, for example, is caused by distraction, not the door [[24:366|AFH 18-17]] [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].

bullets: Fixating on the problem and letting heading, altitude or airspeed wander [[24:107|AFH 5-2]].
Using partial carb heat or turning it off too soon [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].
Not shedding load after an alternator failure, then losing all power when lowering electric flaps or gear [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].
Following a failed gyro instead of cross-checking [[23:332|IFH 11-7]].
Turning the master off for a non-electrical fire and losing radios and transponder [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].
Unbuckling to close an open door, or rushing a low steep turn back to land [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].
Skipping the checklist after doing memory items [[24:36|AFH 1-15]].

check.q: Why can partial carb heat make icing worse?
check.a: If ice is present, partial heat or heat left on too briefly might aggravate the situation [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

scenario.title: Alternator light, then a bang
scenario.setup: You are on a VFR cross-country at 4,500 ft in a trainer with electric flaps, 40 minutes from home and 15 minutes from a towered airport. Late afternoon. The low-voltage light comes on and the ammeter shows a discharge. While you dig for the POH, your passenger's door pops open with a loud bang and wind roar. You flinch and the nose drops 300 ft before you notice.

questions.q: What caused the 300 ft altitude loss, and what is the cure?
questions.a: Startle and distraction, not the airplane. Startle is an automatic reflex to a sudden event [[24:108|AFH 5-3]], and diverted attention can cause an upset [[24:107|AFH 5-2]]. Fly the airplane first; an open door seldom affects the airplane's ability to fly [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

questions.q: Which problem do you handle first, the door or the electrical failure?
questions.a: Leave the door alone and keep belts on [[24:366|AFH 18-17]]. Then run the alternator checklist and shed load; the battery may not last long [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].
The nearer suitable airport. Tell ATC and ask for vectors [[24:363|AFH 18-14]]. Don't continue the flight after the charging system fails [[23:330|IFH 11-5]].

questions.q: What do you plan for the landing?
questions.a: A no-flap landing: the flap motor may drain a weak battery and cause total power loss [[24:362|AFH 18-13]]. Fly a wider, longer pattern and expect up to 50 percent more landing distance [[24:359|AFH 18-10]] [[24:360|AFH 18-11]]. Complete the landing checklist [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

skills.do: When the examiner simulates at least three failures from K1 to K5 (for example rough engine, alternator failure, vacuum failure, smoke, door open), keep control, identify the problem, and state and simulate the correct action.
skills.practice: Chair-fly each failure with the POH. Have your CFI give surprise failures in flight. Use Figure 18-11 to drill gauge readings and causes [[24:365|AFH 18-16]].

skills.do: Find and complete the correct POH emergency or abnormal checklist, using memory items first where the POH has them.
skills.practice: Learn your POH memory items cold. Time yourself finding each checklist page. Do the action, then read to confirm [[24:36|AFH 1-15]] [[24:348|AFH 17-14]].

quiz.q: In an airplane with a constant-speed propeller, the first sign of carburetor ice is usually:
options: A drop in manifold pressure with no rpm change
A rise in cylinder head temperature
quiz.why: The governor holds rpm, so manifold pressure drops instead [[1:170|PHAK 7-10]].

quiz.q: A 25 amp-hour battery feeding a 10-amp load might last about:
quiz.why: AFH example: 5 amps for 5 hours, but only about 2 hours at 10 amps; a 40-amp load might drain it in 10 or 15 minutes [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

quiz.q: After an alternator failure, why expect a no-flap landing in an airplane with electric flaps?
options: Flaps are not allowed after a failure
The flap motor draws high current and may cause total electrical loss
Flaps only work with the alternator
quiz.why: Gear and flap motors use power fast; selecting them on a weak battery may cause an immediate total loss of power [[24:362|AFH 18-13]].

quiz.q: The static port is fully blocked and you descend. The altimeter will:
options: Stay frozen at the blockage altitude
quiz.why: Trapped static pressure freezes the altimeter at the altitude where the blockage occurred [[1:213|PHAK 8-11]].

quiz.q: Unless the POH says otherwise, the first step for an engine compartment fire is to:
options: Dive to blow the fire out
Shut off fuel: mixture idle cutoff and fuel selector off
quiz.why: Shut off fuel to the engine and leave ignition ON to burn off the fuel in the lines [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].

quiz.q: In a split-flap condition the airplane rolls toward:
quiz.why: The roll is toward the wing with the least flap deflection [[24:360|AFH 18-11]].

quiz.q: A cabin door opens right after liftoff. The best action is:
options: Make a tight low turn back to the runway
Climb to pattern altitude, fly a normal pattern and land
Slip toward the door to close it
quiz.why: Don't rush; fly a normal pattern and landing and leave the door alone [[24:366|AFH 18-17]].

quiz.q: A crew pilot at 13,500 ft cabin altitude for 45 minutes must use supplemental oxygen for:
options: The part of the flight over 30 minutes at that altitude
quiz.why: Above 12,500 ft up to and including 14,000 ft, required crew must use oxygen for the part over 30 minutes [[35:401|14 CFR 91.211]].

takeaways: Fly the airplane first; the malfunction rarely kills, the distraction does.
Carb ice: full heat, leave it on until power returns.
Alternator failure: shed load, tell ATC, land at the nearest suitable airport, expect no electric flaps.
Cross-check instruments; cover failed gyros; use the alternate static source.
Engine fire: fuel off, ignition on; electrical fire: isolate the circuit or master off.
Do memory items, then confirm with the POH checklist.
cfi_notes: Examiners must pick at least three items from K1 to K5; cover all, and know the POH memory items for your airplane.
Use Figure 18-11 as flash cards: give the gauge reading, have the student name the cause and action.
Simulate failures without warning (within safety limits) to train startle management, as the AFH recommends scenario-based training with realistic distractions [[24:108|AFH 5-3]].
Students often reach for the master switch for any smoke; stress the radio and transponder trade-off [[24:358|AFH 18-9]].
For glass cockpits, practice reversionary mode and standby-instrument flight; failure modes differ by system and can't all be simulated [[24:365|AFH 18-16]].
gaps: Specific checklists, memory items, limits and system details (alternator reset, emergency gear extension, trim disconnect, oxygen, deice) are POH/AFM specific.
The handbooks do not give a procedure for a jammed or inoperative (non-runaway) trim; only runaway electric trim (AFH 17-14) and using trim after elevator failure (AFH 18-11) are covered.
Turbine-engine power loss causes are not taught here; the Task is written for the airplane used on the practical test.
